title: Hybrid and limitations
sub: Baking and subscenes, what stays on GameObjects, an honest list of downsides, and when ECS is overkill or nearly the only way
cards/0/title: Authoring and Baking: you build the scene from GameObjects
cards/0/body:
Nobody places entities by hand in the Editor. You build the scene from GameObjects as usual, with authoring components (plain MonoBehaviours with fields for designers), and put them into a subscene.

Baking turns them into entities: for each authoring type you write a Baker<T>, and its Bake method gets an entity with GetEntity and attaches components with AddComponent. A prefab reference becomes an entity too — then you can spawn copies of it in the game.

Baking runs in the Editor only, never in the game. While a subscene is open, changes are baked live and incrementally; a closed subscene is fully baked in the background. The build gets a ready-made entity scene: no authoring objects and no conversion at load time.
cards/1/body:
The argument of GetEntity is a TransformUsageFlags value: what this entity needs from a transform. None — data only, no transform; Renderable — drawn but never moves; Dynamic — moves at runtime and gets a LocalTransform. A needless Dynamic on static scenery means extra components and extra work for the transform systems.

At runtime a prefab is already an entity from the baked scene. New copies come from Instantiate, and since that is a structural change, usually through an ECB, as in the previous lesson.
cards/2/q: The game is built. A MonoBehaviour in a regular scene looks for the SpeedAuthoring from a subscene to change the enemies’ speed. What happens?
cards/2/options/0: It finds nothing: the player has no authoring objects from the subscene, only baked entities — change the Speed component instead
cards/2/options/1: It finds it, and the new value is baked on the next frame
cards/2/options/2: It finds it, but the change applies only after the subscene reloads
cards/2/options/3: It finds it: the Baker runs in builds too, just slower
cards/2/explain: Baking is an Editor step. In a build a subscene is ready-made chunks with entities, and there is no GameObject with SpeedAuthoring. At runtime you change the entity’s data, from a system or through EntityManager.
cards/2/wrong/1: Nothing is baked at runtime at all: a Baker is Editor code.
cards/2/wrong/2: Even a reload loads the same baked data: there are no authoring objects in a build.
cards/2/wrong/3: Baking happens in the Editor only — “never in-game”.
cards/3/task: Write a Baker for SpeedAuthoring: a nested class deriving from Baker<SpeedAuthoring>; in Bake get the entity with GetEntity(TransformUsageFlags.Dynamic) — the object moves — and add a Speed component with the value from the metersPerSecond field. The authoring class must have no runtime methods such as Awake, Start or Update.
cards/3/checks/0/label: A nested class derives from Baker<SpeedAuthoring>
cards/3/checks/1/label: public override void Bake(SpeedAuthoring …) is overridden
cards/3/checks/2/label: The entity comes from GetEntity with TransformUsageFlags.Dynamic
cards/3/checks/5/label: No Awake, Start or Update: authoring does not live in the game
cards/3/explain: Authoring is the designer-facing interface in the Editor; the Baker translates it into data. Dynamic, because the object moves at runtime and needs a LocalTransform. The build gets an entity with LocalTransform and Speed, and the MonoBehaviour stays in the Editor.
cards/4/body:
Entities are drawn by the Entities Graphics package. It is not a render pipeline: it works on top of URP or HDRP and feeds them entities with meshes and materials.

Nearly every real Entities project is a hybrid. What usually stays on GameObjects: UI (uGUI, UI Toolkit), the camera, audio, characters driven by an Animator, third-party assets and plugins. The mass simulation goes into entities, the rest stays as it was.

The link runs on the main thread: a MonoBehaviour reads entity data through EntityManager (or a system writes into a GameObject). Such a read waits for the jobs writing that component, so do it late in the frame. For references to Unity objects there are managed components (class … : IComponentData), but they live outside chunks and without Burst.
cards/5/body:
Interviewers value knowing what a tool costs. What is worth naming:

A different model and a learning curve. Data apart from logic, no inheritance and no virtual methods, debugging through the Entities windows (Hierarchy, Systems, Components, Archetypes) rather than the familiar GameObject Inspector.

Ecosystem. Most assets, plugins and built-in Unity systems are built for GameObjects. Entities 1.x has no built-in skeletal animation on the level of Animator — teams use third-party solutions or keep characters on GameObjects.

The Baking layer. Authoring components, bakers, subscenes — one more layer of code to write and maintain.

New performance bugs. Structural changes and sync points, needless archetypes, enableable components where they do not belong.

API history. The move from Entities 0.51 to 1.0 changed the API a lot: conversion gave way to Baking, and Translation/Rotation to LocalTransform. Old tutorials mislead.
cards/6/q: Which of these are honest limitations of Entities? Select all that apply.
cards/6/options/0: Most assets and built-in systems (UI, Animator, audio) are built for GameObjects — you need a hybrid
cards/6/options/1: The move from Entities 0.51 to 1.0 changed the API a lot; old tutorials are out of date
cards/6/options/2: Structural changes and sync points are a new class of performance problems
cards/6/options/3: Entities Graphics is a separate render pipeline; URP and HDRP are not needed with it
cards/6/options/4: An Entities project cannot contain a single GameObject
cards/6/explain: Entities Graphics works on top of URP or HDRP, not instead of them. And a hybrid is the norm: UI, the camera, audio and animated characters often stay on GameObjects.
cards/7/title: When ECS is overkill, and when it is nearly the only way
cards/7/body:
Overkill when there are hundreds of objects, each with its own unique logic, the game rests on UI and story, the team does not know Entities and the deadline is tight. If the Profiler shows one hot spot, a Burst job over a NativeArray inside an ordinary MonoBehaviour manager closes it — without rewriting the project.

Nearly the only way when tens of thousands of similar objects are not only drawn but alive: each has movement, logic, collisions, networking. Crowds, RTS units, projectiles, ecosystems. Then the cost of thousands of GameObjects (Transforms, Update calls, scattered data) becomes the main problem, and no single job removes it. Add large worlds that stream subscenes and networked games on Netcode for Entities.

The interview formula: “Jobs + Burst for the hot loop, Entities when the whole world is hot”.
cards/8/q: A mobile puzzle game: 200 objects, each with its own logic. In the Profiler one pathfinding loop eats 4 ms per frame. What do you suggest?
cards/8/options/0: Move that loop into a Burst job over a NativeArray and leave the rest on GameObjects
cards/8/options/1: Move the project to Entities: on mobile it is a must
cards/8/options/2: Rewrite every MonoBehaviour as an ISystem so the logic runs in jobs
cards/8/options/3: Nothing: 4 ms on mobile is normal
cards/8/explain: There is one clear hot spot — treat that. 200 objects do not strain a GameObject architecture, and moving to Entities is expensive and adds almost nothing here.
cards/8/wrong/1: It is not a must: Entities pays off on masses of similar objects, and here there are 200.
cards/8/wrong/2: A huge amount of work for one spot that a single job closes.
cards/8/wrong/3: In a 16.6 ms frame (60 FPS), 4 ms for one loop is a quarter of the budget; worth fixing.
cards/9/q: An RTS: 50,000 units, each with movement, avoidance, shooting and rendering. The GameObject version cannot hold the frame rate, and the time is smeared over thousands of Update calls and transforms. What do you suggest?
cards/9/options/0: Entities: units as entities from baked prefabs, logic in systems with Burst-compiled IJobEntity, rendering by Entities Graphics, UI on GameObjects
cards/9/options/1: A Burst job for the heaviest loop — that will be enough
cards/9/options/2: An object pool, so units are not created anew
cards/9/explain: Here the whole world is hot: the cost is in the thousands of GameObjects and the scattered data themselves. Entities removes it entirely — data in chunks, logic in jobs, drawing without GameObjects.
cards/9/wrong/1: One job removes one spot, while the time is smeared over the Update calls and transforms of 50,000 objects.
cards/9/wrong/2: A pool removes the cost of creation, not the cost of every frame the objects live.
cards/9/wrong/3: Threads do not help code that runs on the main thread in Update.
cards/10/q: Interviewer: “Why didn’t you move the project to ECS?” Which answer is stronger?
cards/10/options/0: “The Profiler showed one hot spot, a Burst job closed it, and we fit the frame budget. Moving to Entities would have meant redoing the UI links and animation — the cost was higher than the gain”
cards/10/options/1: “ECS is still raw, nobody uses it”
cards/10/options/2: “The lead decided, I didn’t look into it”
cards/10/options/3: “ECS is always faster, we just had no time”
cards/10/explain: A strong answer shows a measurement, a decision based on cost and gain, and awareness of the limitations. The others are either wrong or say you never thought about the question.
